title: David's Last Song and His Heroes
overview: This chapter gives a final poem attributed to David about good rule and God's lasting promise, then lists the elite warriors who fought for him and some of their famous deeds.

parts.label: David's last words (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: David presents this poem as a message from God, not just his own opinion. It says a ruler who is fair and respects God is like sunrise on a cloudless morning, or the bright sun after rain that makes fresh grass spring up.

parts.label: A lasting promise (vv. 5-7)
parts.note: The "covenant" is the binding promise God made earlier that David's descendants would keep ruling. Translations differ on whether verse 5 is a confident question or David admitting his family falls short, and the wicked are pictured as thorns no one handles bare-handed, fit only for burning.

parts.label: The Three and their stands (vv. 8-12)
parts.note: These were David's top warriors, famous for holding their ground against the Philistines, Israel's main enemy, when others ran. The Hebrew of verse 8 is hard to read, so the names and details there are uncertain, and the text credits the victories to the LORD.

parts.label: Water from Bethlehem (vv. 13-17)
parts.note: While David hid in a cave, his hometown of Bethlehem was held by the Philistines, and three men broke through their lines to fetch him water from its well. David refused to drink what had risked their lives and poured it out to the LORD instead, treating it like blood, which in Israel belonged to God alone.

parts.label: Abishai and Benaiah (vv. 18-23)
parts.note: These two commanders were honored above most fighters but still ranked below the first Three. Benaiah, known for killing a lion in a pit on a snowy day, was put over David's personal guard and later became army chief under David's son Solomon.

parts.label: The Thirty (vv. 24-39)
parts.note: This roll of honor includes foreigners such as an Ammonite and a Hittite, and the count of thirty-seven seems to include leaders named earlier. It ends with Uriah the Hittite, the loyal soldier David had arranged to be killed so he could take Uriah's wife, Bathsheba.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the just ruler and everlasting promise in verses 3 to 5 directly predict Jesus, or describe the ideal king of David's line that they later saw fulfilled in him.
think: This list of heroes ends by naming Uriah, a loyal man the king himself wronged. What do you make of a story that honors its hero and still refuses to leave out the person he harmed?
